transcript.text: indesit oven stoped heating, fan goes round n light on but its stone cold after 20 mins. grill werks fine tho. any ideas b4 i call some1 out

Yes, and the good news is your description already narrows it down a lot. So the problem is in the part that heats the fan oven specifically. 1. The fan oven element (the round ring element hidden behind the back panel, around the fan) has burnt out. This is by far the most common cause of exactly this pattern on Indesit and most other fan ovens.
2. A simple setting issue: the defrost setting runs the fan and light with no heat, and some ovens won't heat after a power cut until the clock is set to manual.
3. Less often, a burnt connector on the element's wires, or the selector switch or thermostat not switching the element on. 1. Check the function knob is on the fan symbol with a ring around it, not just a plain fan (that's often defrost), light-only or eco. Turn the temperature knob up and see if the temperature light comes on. If it was on the wrong setting, that's your answer.
2. Look at the clock. If it's flashing or showing an auto/timer symbol (often after a power cut), set the time and select manual. On many models that's the hand symbol or two buttons held together; your manual will show how. Then try 180°C on fan for 15 minutes.
3. If that makes no difference, listen as you turn the temperature knob up from off. A faint click suggests the thermostat is switching, which points back towards the element or its wiring.
4. Optional, with the oven cold and switched off at the cooker switch: remove the shelves and the back panel inside the oven (usually a few screws) and look at the ring element. A visible split, blister or burnt spot suggests it. If it looks fine, it could still have failed inside, or the fault could be in the connectors or switch. If the settings are right and it still won't heat, a failed fan element is the best bet, but I'd keep the connectors and selector switch in mind. On many models the element can be changed from inside the oven. If you're not comfortable working on mains-connected wiring, an engineer can confirm the cause with a meter in a few minutes. It's normally a reasonably cheap repair, so usually worth doing rather than replacing the oven. What did you find with the knob setting and the clock?
clock is set n on manual, nothing flashing. the orange temp light comes on n stays on. still no heat on fan setting tho

That's useful, and it rules out the free fixes. The timer isn't blocking it. The orange light staying on means the thermostat is asking for heat and never reaching temperature. So the problem is probably in the circuit that feeds the ring element behind the fan. 1. This is by far the most common cause of this exact pattern, and I'd put it well ahead of the others.
2. A burnt or loose wire connector on the element's terminals.
3. Less likely, a worn contact in the function selector switch that isn't sending power to the element on the fan setting. 1. Switch off at the cooker isolator switch on the wall (or the fuse box) and let the oven cool fully. Take out the shelves and undo the screws on the back panel inside the oven. Look at the ring element. A split, blister, bubble or burnt spot on it suggests the element.
2. If the element looks fine, you'll usually find its terminals poke through the rear wall. They can often be reached by undoing the element's fixing screws and easing it forward gently. Look at the wires on the terminals. Brown, scorched or melted connectors point to the wiring, which often goes along with a failed element.
3. Only if you're confident with a multimeter, and the cooker is still isolated: disconnect the element and measure across its two terminals. A healthy fan element typically reads a few tens of ohms. No reading at all (open circuit) means it has failed, even if it looks perfect. If the element tests good and the connectors are clean, the selector switch becomes the suspect. That sits behind the control panel, so it's better left to an engineer. Swapping a fan element is usually a fairly cheap job and normally worth doing rather than replacing the oven. If you'd rather not handle the wiring, an engineer can confirm it with a meter in minutes. What do you see when you get the back panel off?
ok isolated it at the wall switch n took the back panel off. theres a blister/split in the ring element near the bottom wiv a black mark. also heard a small pop from in there last time it worked

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. That settles it. A split or blister with a black burn mark, plus the pop you heard the last time it worked, is a common sign of a fan oven element that has burst. The pop is the moment the element shorted through its outer sheath. Your earlier checks back this up: the fan turns, the temperature light stays on because the thermostat is calling for heat, and the clock is in manual. I'm fairly sure the ring element is the failed part. Because it has shorted and burnt, please leave the oven switched off at the wall switch and don't use it, grill included, until a qualified engineer has checked it. When an element blows like this, the wires and push-on connectors where it joins the back wall can get scorched too. Those need checking and replacing if they're damaged, along with the element. An engineer will also confirm the rest of the circuit is sound before it goes back into use. The repair itself is usually straightforward and fairly cheap, so it's normally well worth doing rather than replacing the oven. To get the right element, I need the model number. It's usually on a label on the frame around the door opening, visible when the door is open. It may also be on the back or underside of the oven. If you can't get to it right now, that's fine, it can wait until it's convenient.
[Panel: "To check a suitable replacement — Enter your model number below. Once we have the model I can check whether a suitable replacement is available. It's usually on a sticker inside the door or around the frame, or on the back of the appliance."]
its on the rating plate on the door frame, IFW 6330 IX. so is the element somethin i can swap myself or do i need an engineer?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Honest answer: in this case, get an engineer. On many fan ovens the ring element is a fairly simple swap from inside the cavity, just a few screws behind the back panel, so on a straightforward failure it's a job a confident DIYer can do. Yours isn't straightforward, though. It went with a pop and left a black burn mark, so it shorted rather than just going open circuit. When that happens the push-on connectors and the wiring behind the back wall can get scorched or heat-damaged. That needs a qualified engineer to inspect it and check the circuit before the oven is used again, and that includes the grill. The connectors or wiring are the next thing that may need replacing along with it. So the most sensible route is to have an engineer fit the element and check the wiring in the same visit. That way the fault is confirmed and the oven is passed as safe in one go. Give them the model number from the rating plate (IFW 6330 IX) so they can bring the correct element. Ask them to check the element's terminals and wiring, and the selector switch, while they're there. Until then, keep it switched off at the wall switch. It's usually a modest repair, so it's normally well worth doing rather than replacing the oven.
